title: Do not let a live internal collection escape, and do not mutate a caller's collection by side effect
summary: Lists and dicts are shared references. Returning a live value you own is not a snapshot: the caller can mutate your internals. Mutating an argument (append/.sort/in-place update) writes back into the caller's object. An LLM reproduces both: it exposes engine-held lists to callers or sorts an input list it was only asked to read, silently altering the owner's state.
semantics: Assignment, parameter passing and return store a reference, not a copy. Methods like .append, .sort, .update, .clear mutate the referred object in place; sorted() and dict(...) create copies.
why_this_is_an_article: Whether mutation is harmful needs to know ownership and intent; there is no safe global claim like 'never sort()'.
evidence_note: PLABEL: canonical CPython container reference semantics.
invariants: When you return stored state, return value.copy() / list(...) / dict(...) / Sorted-named read view if callers should not alter your internal memory.
When you only need to read an input collection, do not mutate it; copy first then mutate locally if needed.
Prefer sorted(x) and a new dict/list for derived results rather than sorting an argument in place unless the parameter contract explicitly allows an in-place sort.
Document clearly when a method intentionally mutates a container in place.
